n: In this lecture we consider the fundamentals of thanatology. Life and death are inseparably linked: death is the logical end of life. Just as there is no life without death, so there is no death without life. The first direction is determining the time of death; it is based on postmortem changes, supravital reactions of tissues and laboratory investigations. The second direction is euthanasia; its original meaning is relieving the suffering of terminally ill patients, and four types are distinguished. The third direction is the basis of transplantation: between death of the cerebral cortex and death of other organs there is an intermediate period of about 20 hours.

Thanatology: concept and sections. The term "thanatology" was introduced into medicine by I. I. Mechnikov. From the Greek thanatos, the name of the god of death, and logos, doctrine; that is, the doctrine of death. As a component of biology it studies the process of dying, determination of the fact of death, causes of death, postmortem changes, burial and preservation. General thanatology considers the general aspects of the questions, while particular thanatology considers them from the standpoint of specific types of death. Forensic thanatology studies these questions in order to resolve the questions arising in the work of the inquiry, investigation and court bodies.

t: The process of dying: the chain of terminal states
n: The process of dying consists of a chain of terminal states: preagony, terminal pause, agony, clinical death and biological death. Agony is the last attempt to return to life; at its end, first breathing and then the heartbeat stops. Clinical death usually lasts 5–6 minutes; at low temperature it may extend to 30 minutes. Attention: clinical death is not the same as biological death. In the first, function can be restored; in the second, it cannot.

Preagony and terminal pause. In preagony the higher parts of the central nervous system, that is, the CNS, are inhibited, circulation and breathing are sharply disturbed, and consciousness is clouded or lost. Acidosis and hypoxia develop in the tissues, and blood pressure falls. The pulse is found only in the carotid and femoral arteries; the skin pales and dyspnoea occurs. Preagony may last from several minutes to several days. In the terminal pause breathing suddenly stops, cardiac activity is sharply disturbed, and the pupil dilates and does not respond to light; this state lasts from several seconds to 3–4 minutes.

Agony and facies hippocratica. Agony lasts from several minutes to several days; at its end, first breathing and then the heartbeat stops. The higher centres of the brain are inhibited and control is lost. Their function is taken over by the imperfect centres lying lower in the brain. Breathing is restored, blood pressure rises somewhat, sometimes to subnormal, and the pulse begins to be detected. This is regarded as the last attempt to return to life. Facies hippocratica: the face pales and takes on an earthy hue, the eyeballs sink, the lower jaw sags and the mouth falls open.

Clinical death and biological death. Clinical death begins after the heart stops and usually lasts up to 5–6 minutes. At low temperature it may extend to 30 minutes; disease, age and health also have an influence. The chain is as follows: agony, the heart stops, clinical death, irreversible change in the cortex, biological death. The possibility of return became the basis of resuscitation; in biological death an irreversible change occurs in the brain.

t: Rapid and slow death; four types of agony
n: Rapid and slow death; four types of agony. Examples of rapid death are electrical injury, mechanical asphyxia and anaphylactic shock. Slow death comprises states associated with various diseases. W. Lawes and S. Berg in 1965 divided agony by duration into four types: no agony, short agony, long agony and artificially prolonged. In short agony it lasts 4–5 minutes and is seen in asphyxia and electrical injury. Long agony lasts several hours or days. Artificially prolonged agony lasts weeks, months or years with the help of medical procedures. Attention: death without agony is not the same as death with short agony.

Quick questions on terminal states. First question: how long does preagony last? Answer: from several minutes to several days. Second question: what stops in the terminal pause, and how long does it last? Answer: breathing suddenly stops; from several seconds to 3–4 minutes. Third question: when does clinical death begin and how many minutes does it usually last? Answer: after the heart stops; up to 5–6 minutes. Fourth question: how long can clinical death extend at low temperature? Answer: up to 30 minutes.

t: Case analysis: identifying the stage of a terminal state
n: Case analysis: identifying the stage of a terminal state. Situation: in a patient, breathing has suddenly stopped, cardiac activity is sharply disturbed, and the pupils are dilated and do not respond to light. Which stage is this? Answer: the terminal pause; it lasts from several seconds to 3–4 minutes. The next stage is agony: breathing is restored, blood pressure rises somewhat, and the pulse is detected. This is the last attempt to return to life. Is it possible to bring a person back to life after the heart has stopped? In clinical death it is, usually within 5–6 minutes, because later the changes in the cortex are irreversible.

t: Euthanasia: the term and its essence
n: Euthanasia: the term and its essence. The term "euthanasia" was introduced in the 16th century by the English philosopher F. Bacon. In Greek, eu means good and thanatos death; the term means "good death". The original meaning of euthanasia is relieving the suffering of terminally ill patients. However, many understand the concept narrowly and include in it only active and passive euthanasia.

Four types of euthanasia are distinguished: active, passive, medicothanasia and dysthanasia. In active euthanasia death is hastened by an action; it has direct and indirect forms. Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, is the limitation or cessation of medical aid; in criminal law it is assessed as improper performance of official duty. In medicothanasia suffering is relieved with drugs, and the aim is quality of life. In dysthanasia life is prolonged to the maximum, by palliative and radical treatment. Attention: orthothanasia is not the same as dysthanasia.

Active euthanasia: direct and indirect. Active euthanasia is hastening death by a particular action. The difference lies in the aim: in the direct form there is an intention to hasten death, in the indirect form there is no such aim. In the direct form the assessment is homicide or suicide, in the indirect form negligence or accident. Example: to reduce pain, a drug is administered by the physician in a large dose, or taken by the patient.

Passive euthanasia, medicothanasia and dysthanasia. Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, is the limitation or cessation of aid to a terminally ill patient; in criminal law it counts as failure to perform official duty. Medicothanasia is relieving the suffering of a terminally ill patient with drugs and improving the quality of life as far as possible. Dysthanasia is prolonging the patient's life to the maximum while relieving suffering, not only by palliative but also by radical treatment. Many understand euthanasia narrowly: only the active and passive forms are included, that is, hastening death actively or passively.

t: Case analysis: distinguishing the type of euthanasia
n: Case analysis: distinguishing the type of euthanasia. Situation: to reduce the pain of a terminally ill patient, the physician administered an analgesic in a large dose. There was no aim of hastening death. Which type is this? It is indirect active euthanasia; if death occurs, it is assessed as causing death by negligence or as an accident. Compare: in direct active euthanasia there is the aim of hastening death, and it appears as homicide or suicide. Attention: the difference lies in the presence or absence of the aim of hastening death. Cessation of aid, by contrast, is the passive type.

t: Establishing that death has occurred: phylogenetic age
n: Establishing that death has occurred: phylogenetic age. The phylogenetic age of organs and tissues differs, so irreversible changes do not occur in them at the same time. The higher the phylogenetic age, the more sensitive the tissue; therefore an irreversible change occurs first in the cerebral cortex. Death of the cortex, according to Durwald, 1981, is "individual death"; the organism loses the property of wholeness. The chain is as follows: irreversible change in the cortex, integrative activity is disturbed, brain death is regarded as biological death, an intermediate period of about 20 hours, then the possibility of transplantation.

t: Brain death and the basis of transplantation
n: Brain death and the basis of transplantation. Death of the cerebral cortex is the beginning of biological death and is accepted as "brain death"; the organism then loses the property of wholeness. The intermediate period between death of the cortex and death of other organs and tissues is about 20 hours. During this time their function may continue or be restored. The removal of organs and tissues from a dead body for transplantation is based on this feature. The earlier after biological death organs and tissues are removed, the more effective the result of transplantation.

t: Procedure for establishing brain death and legal consequences
n: Procedure for establishing brain death and legal consequences. Brain death is established in a set procedure; this procedure is developed by the Ministry of Health. In treatment institutions brain death is usually established by appropriately qualified resuscitation specialists and neurologists. The process requires certain apparatus and equipment. If these are absent, biological death is established mainly by postmortem changes. In most countries, by law, in this case it is permitted to stop resuscitation and to remove organs and tissues from the dead body.

t: Early and reliable signs of death
n: Early and reliable signs of death. Early signs, although detected immediately after death, are only probable: immobility, pallor of the skin, absence of breathing and heartbeat. The earliest reliable sign is the Beloglazov symptom, that is, the "cat's eye"; it is detected after 15–20 minutes. Other reliable signs: cooling of the body to 23 °C and below, cadaveric lividity, rigor and drying. Attention: slight cooling of the body is a probable sign, whereas cooling to 23 °C and below is a reliable sign.

t: Quick question: signs for establishing death
n: Quick questions on signs for establishing death. First question: to which group of signs do immobility of the body, pallor of the skin, and absence of breathing and heartbeat belong? Answer: early, that is, probable signs. Second question: what is the earliest reliable sign, and when is it detected? Answer: the Beloglazov symptom, "cat's eye", after 15–20 minutes. Third question: what shape does the pupil take when the eyeball is compressed from the sides in the Beloglazov symptom? Answer: an oval shape. Attention: an early sign is not a reliable sign. Cooling of the body to 23 °C and below, cadaveric lividity, rigor and drying are reliable signs.

t: Case analysis: brain death and organ removal
n: Case analysis: brain death and organ removal. Situation: in a patient in the intensive care unit, death of the cerebral cortex has been established, while the function of other organs is for the time being continuing. Between death of the cortex and death of other organs there is an interval of about 20 hours; transplantation is based precisely on this feature. In most countries this state counts as biological death; by law it is permitted to stop resuscitation and remove organs. Why are organs removed early, and who establishes brain death? If removed early, the result is effective; the establishment is carried out by the resuscitation specialist and neurologist in the procedure set by the ministry.

Forensic classification of death. Violent death results from external action, non-violent death from diseases. Kinds of violent death: homicide, suicide and accident. The classification has three levels: category, kind and type. The category, that is, violent or non-violent, is determined by the forensic medical expert. Determining the kind is within the competence of law-enforcement bodies, since it rests on establishing intent. The type, that is, the type of external action or disease, is again determined by the forensic medical expert.

t: Supravital reactions: mechanical and electrical action
n: Supravital reactions: mechanical and electrical action. Mechanical action is usually applied to the shoulder muscle with the handle of a neurological hammer or a metal ruler. Muscle contraction lasts 1–2 hours, and the ridge-shaped swelling up to 10. Attention: the idiomuscular swelling is not muscle contraction but a ridge-shaped swelling at the site of action. With electrical action the muscles of the face and limbs respond for 2–3 hours, the orbicularis oris for 3–5 hours, and only the eye muscles up to 11–12. With a needle electrode, the pupil: 0–6 hours constriction; 7–12 hours constriction and deformation; up to 30 hours deformation.

Supravital reactions: chemical action. If 1 % atropine is dropped into the eye in the first 5–6 hours after death, the pupil dilates; under the action of 1 % pilocarpine it constricts. If a solution, 0.1 ml, is introduced with a fine needle into the anterior chamber of the eye, the reaction is detected up to 24 hours; the pupil diameter and the duration of change are measured. In the sweat gland test the skin is smeared with a 2 % alcoholic solution of iodine, starch and castor oil, and 1 % adrenaline or 2 % pilocarpine, 1 ml, is injected under the skin. After 0.5–1.0 hours a blue spot appears due to sweating; the method is used within 30 hours after death.

Classification of postmortem changes. Early changes appear on the first day, and late changes from the second day. Early changes include cooling, drying, lividity, rigor and autolysis. Late destructive changes are putrefaction and the action of insects, animals, birds and fish. Late preservative changes are mummification, adipocere and peat tanning. Freezing is also possible in natural conditions. Artificial changes: dismemberment, burning and dissolution are destructive; embalming and freezing are preservative. They do not depend on the time of death. Attention: autolysis is an early change, and putrefaction a late destructive change; do not confuse them.

Cooling of the body. Thermoregulation is disturbed: heat is not produced, loss continues, and the body cools. External factors: air temperature, humidity, wind, clothing. Internal factors: age, nutrition, cause and rate of death. In room conditions the temperature falls by about 1 °C per hour. Thermometry is carried out in the mouth, axilla, rectum and liver. Equalisation of temperature with the environment occurs after 16 hours in the axilla, after 19 hours in the rectum and after 25 hours in the liver.

Drying of the body. Drying is related to cessation of glandular secretion and evaporation of moisture. First the moist places dry, that is, the vermilion border of the lips, the mucous membranes and the cornea. If the eyes are open: in 1–3 hours the cornea clouds, and in 4–5 hours a triangular brownish Larche spot appears in the conjunctiva. Injured areas dry and become firmer than the surrounding skin, yellowish-brown; these are parchment spots. Retraction of the skin gives the impression that hair and nails are growing. Attention: a parchment spot is not an abrasion sustained during life. If gauze with warm physiological saline is applied for 5–10 minutes, the parchment softens and pales, while an abrasion does not change.

Rigor mortis. A decrease in ATP, that is, adenosine triphosphate, leads to rigor; an increase in calcium is also important. The dynamics: at 1–3 hours it is first detected in the masticatory muscles, at 12–16 hours rigor is present in all muscles, at 24 hours it is at maximum, and at 3–7 days it disappears completely. Rigor broken early is restored more weakly, and then is not restored: this shows that the position of the body has been changed. Cataleptic rigor appears at once in all muscles: in injury of the medulla oblongata, convulsive poisoning or disease.

Cadaveric lividity: three stages. After the heart stops, the blood flows under gravity into the vessels of the lower parts of the body. The first stage is hypostasis, beginning at 1.5–2 hours; it disappears on pressure, is quickly restored, and if the position is changed appears in the new dependent area. Hypostasis lasts up to 8–12 hours; red cells number 6–7 million/mm³, and in the stasis stage up to 8–10 million. Stasis, 12–24 hours: it pales on pressure, is restored slowly, and if the position is changed appears partly in the new area. Imbibition occurs through putrefaction: the colour does not change, and it does not appear in a new place. There is no clear time boundary between the stages; they pass gradually into one another.

Cadaveric lividity and bruise: distinction. Lividity lies in the dependent parts of the body, its boundary is indistinct, it merges, and disappears or pales on pressure. A bruise lies in various parts of the body, has a definite shape, does not merge, and does not change colour on pressure. On cross-section, drops of blood are found in lividity, or fat soaked with blood in imbibition, whereas in a bruise clotted blood is found. The colour depends on death: in rapid death dark reddish-bluish, in carbon monoxide pinkish-red, in cyanide cherry. Attention: lividity is not a bruise. If wrongly assessed, it may lead to an unjustified examination and exhumation.

Quick questions on early postmortem changes. First question: when does rigor mortis begin to be detected, and in which muscles does it begin? Answer: after 1–3 hours, first in the masticatory muscles. Second question: when does rigor reach its maximum, and when does it disappear completely? Answer: maximum after 24 hours; it disappears completely in 3–7 days. Third question: by how much does the body temperature fall per hour in room conditions? Answer: about one degree. Fourth question: when does lividity appear, and how long does stasis last? Answer: after 1.5–2 hours; stasis 12–24 hours.

t: Autolysis and putrefaction; decomposition of the body
n: Autolysis and putrefaction; decomposition of the body. Autolysis is the self-digestion of tissue by cellular enzymes after death; it begins on the first day and may resemble the action of a corrosive poison. Putrefaction proceeds well from +20 °C to +40 °C and stops at sub-zero temperature and above +55 °C. Casper's ratio is 1:2:8: in water it is 2 times, and in earth 8 times, slower than in air. Signs: green discoloration on day 2, putrefactive venous pattern on days 3–4, emphysema and blisters on days 4–6. Types: gaseous, moist and dry. Fly larvae appear after 24–30 hours at room temperature. Insects help to determine the time, whereas destruction by animals and birds is of no use for this.

Late preservative and artificial changes. In these cases putrefaction stops, and traces of injury and the external appearance may be preserved. Mummification occurs in a warm, dry, ventilated place, 6–12 months; in a child 4–6 months. Adipocere forms in a damp place or in water, with little air, in cooler conditions, 10–12 months; in a child 4–5 months. Peat tanning occurs in a peat bog under the action of humic acids and preserves for many years. Freezing occurs at natural low temperature. In embalming, ethyl alcohol with formalin, in equal parts, is injected into the femoral artery and cavities. Dismemberment is divided into defensive, that is, concealment, and offensive, that is, revenge; complete burning takes 20 hours in an adult and 2–3 hours in a child.

t: Methods of determining time of death
n: Methods of determining time of death. In room conditions the temperature falls by about 1 °C per hour. Rectal thermometry is carried out at least twice; there are also formulas and tables. The lividity is pressed with a force of 196 kPa for 3 seconds and the time of colour recovery is measured; the table differs according to the type of death. Supravital reactions, that is, muscular, pupillary and sweat gland, laboratory indicators such as potassium content, and analysis of insects are used. So far there is no single reliable method, so many methods are used. In the first 1–2 days the accuracy is a few hours, later days, and from the skeleton months and years.

Rectal thermometry table, Bilkun, 1985. The rectal temperature of the body falls in accordance with the time of death: by the table, at 2 hours 38.5 °C, at 6 hours 32.8 °C, at 12 hours 29.2 °C, at 18 hours 26.2 °C, at 24 hours 23.2 °C, at 29 hours 20.9 °C. The temperature is measured in the rectum; thermometry is carried out at least twice at a certain interval. Formulas based on cooling, Fiddes-Patten and Burmann, and nomograms have also been developed. The rectal temperature equals the ambient temperature 30–31 hours after death.

Lividity colour recovery time, Kononenko table. The lividity is pressed with a force of 196 kPa for 3 seconds and the time of colour recovery is measured. In rapidly occurring death at 2 hours the colour recovers in 9–10 seconds, at 6 hours in 20–28 seconds, at 12 hours in 55–62 seconds. In agonal death at 2 hours 5–6 seconds, at 6 hours 21–33 seconds, at 12 hours 46–58 seconds. The table differs according to the type and cause of death: mechanical asphyxia, alcohol poisoning, blood loss.

t: Time since death by laboratory and other signs
n: Time since death by laboratory and other signs. In cerebrospinal fluid and the vitreous body of the eye, the potassium content rises and the sodium content falls. By the end of the first day glycogen disappears from the liver, and after 12 hours ATP activity disappears from the tissues. Sperm are motile up to 10 hours and sluggish up to 24 hours. Autolysis in the internal organs begins to be detected after 12–18 hours and becomes very marked after 36–48 hours. The species and stage of development of insects are examined; they are preserved in ethyl ether or formalin and sent for entomological examination. Of the external signs, from 6–8 days a plant pales.

t: Case analysis: time since death from rectal temperature
n: Case analysis: time since death from rectal temperature. The rectal temperature was measured as +30 °C at 10 o'clock and +28.2 °C at 12 o'clock. In two hours the body cooled by 1.8 °C, that is, about 0.9 °C per hour. In the example, death occurred 7–7.5 hours before 10 o'clock. Remember: thermometry is carried out at least twice.

t: Stages and document of forensic medical examination of the body
n: Stages and document of forensic medical examination of the body. The examination is ordered in violent death or suspicion of it, an unknown person, or an objection to medical care. The stages: review of the materials, external examination, internal examination, that is, 3 cavities, the diagnosis and death certificate, then laboratory investigations and findings. The expert's conclusion consists of an introduction, investigation and findings. The diagnosis and findings are signed only by the expert. The body is released not later than 1 day; in difficult cases storage in the morgue for up to 3 days is guaranteed.

Forensic and pathological autopsy. A real autopsy differs in principle as forensic or pathological; there are also verbal and virtual autopsies. A forensic medical examination is carried out to confirm or exclude signs of violence, on the basis of a ruling or court order; the expert gives a receipt, the time of death is established, and the conclusion is given to the person who ordered it. A pathological examination is carried out to check the correctness of treatment, on the instruction of the head of the institution; no receipt is required, the time of death is in the case history, and the protocol is attached to the case history. In a verbal autopsy the body is not opened; a virtual autopsy is based on tomography and is so far carried out only in scientific institutions.

Conclusion and main theses. The time of death is determined mainly from cooling of the body and cadaveric lividity. There is no single reliable method, so many methods are used. Euthanasia: active, that is, direct and indirect, and passive, that is, orthothanasia; medicothanasia and dysthanasia are also distinguished. In the narrow sense only active and passive. Death of the cerebral cortex is regarded as the beginning of biological death; the interval to death of other organs is about 20 hours. If the law permits, after brain death organs and tissues are removed for transplantation. The earlier they are removed, the more effective the result.
